newsitem.title: USA: Low US food inflation seen '97, maybe 2.4 pct - USDA.
newsitem.headline: Low US food inflation seen '97, maybe 2.4 pct - USDA.

text.p: U.S. food prices will rise minimally this year, perhaps no more than 2.4 percent, a relief from last year's 3.3 percent -- the biggest one-year gain of the decade, the Agriculture Department said Monday.

"Retail food prices...are projected to rise less than the general inflation rate, continuing a long-term trend," the department said in papers released at its annual Outlook Forum. It pegged inflation at 3.2 percent for this year but also said food inflation would average only 2.4 percent a year for the coming decade.

The food inflation forecast was set at two to four percent, a reduction from the initial three to four percent. The department traditionally sets a wide range in the early months of the year and narrows it as the year progresses.

Economist Annette Clauson, the department's forecaster, said food price increases would be "probably lower" than last year. Ample grain and beef supplies would reduce the chance of an upsurge, she said.
Americans spend nearly half of all their food dollars on restaurant and take-out food. Keen competition will cut hold price increases to a minimum, she said.

Pork, fresh fruits and vegetables, and cereals and bakery products were forecast to record the largest increases this year, but still in the range of three to five percent. Eggs skyrocketed 18 percent last year, pork zoomed 9.9 percent and fresh fruits climbed 7.1 percent.

James MacDonald, a colleague of Clauson, said in prepared remarks that flaws in the Consumer Price Index for food resulted in a 30 percent-40 percent overstatement of food inflation since 1978. The Bureau of Labor Statistics was making changes to eliminate a sizable part of the overstatement, he said.
